value.region_notes_beginner: Eggplant is a stretch crop west of the Cascades: our summers rarely get hot enough to make it easy. Pick your sunniest, most sheltered spot, warm the soil with black plastic, and choose a fast variety like Fairy Tale, Patio Baby, or Ichiban. On the immediate coast summers run even cooler, so treat eggplant as a bonus crop: start later, plant out in June, and give it a cold frame or row cover if you can.
value.region_notes_seasoned: Eggplant is the marginal warm-season crop here, the weakest fit of the garden nightshades for the maritime PNW's cool, marine-tempered summer. In the valley, site it in full sun with reflected heat, warm the soil ahead of transplanting, and lean on a fast, small-fruited variety; harvest realistically runs early August into mid October, closing well before the first frost as cool, wet weather stalls fruit sizing. On the coast, delay transplanting into June, pick the single warmest microsite available, and consider a tunnel or cloche, per WSU's guidance (EM057E) that eggplant needs the most supplemental warmth of the common vegetables; treat any coastal harvest as a bonus, not a given.

harvest_end.label: primary

8.zone_notes: This is a genuinely marginal corn climate: the Willamette Valley's moderate summer heat lets early to midseason su/se hybrids finish, but a late or supersweet (sh2) type often will not. OSU Extension's Oregon planting-date table gives this valley region an April-into-June direct-sow window (EM9027); stagger a fresh block every two weeks within it, in the warmest, most open bed you have.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: OSU Extension's Oregon planting-date table (EM9027) marks sweet potato "not suitable" for planting in EITHER the Willamette Valley or the coast. This is not a season-LENGTH problem (the maritime PNW's frost-free window is long enough on paper); it is a season-HEAT problem: sweet potato needs sustained summer warmth to bulk its roots, and the region's marine-tempered summer rarely supplies it. Set slips only once the soil is reliably above about 65°F, warm the ridge with black plastic mulch, and site the planting in the single hottest, most sheltered spot available; a low tunnel over the row for the first several weeks helps. Even with every advantage, expect small, light roots rather than a full Southern-style crop (OSU / WSU).

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Dig well before the first fall frost, which kills the vines and lets cold damage the roots in the ground.

The January planting leans on the coast's exceptionally mild, marine-buffered winter, well ahead of the coast's own average last frost in late March; cauliflower transplants tolerate the coast's typically light frosts once hardened off. Neither zone needs a summer heat pause, but cauliflower is fussier than cabbage about steady growth: a cold check or moisture stress causes small, premature button curds rather than one good head, so keep it growing without a stall in either zone.

You get peppery leaves within weeks and flowers from early summer clear into fall, since our cool, mild summer suits this crop rather than working against it. Grow it lean (no fertilizer) for the best flower show, and use a sacrificial patch to trap aphids away from vegetables. Watch for slugs in the wet shoulder seasons.

Favor faster single-stem or mid-size types over the slowest giant varieties, which can struggle to fully ripen a head before fall rain and the first frost arrive. There is no heat pause here (there is rarely too much heat to begin with); stake tall types against coastal wind and watch for downy mildew in a cool, wet spring.

Shear tired plants back partway through the season to reflush a fresh round of bloom. It self-sows freely and is a reliable insectary plant near cool-season vegetables, drawing hoverflies and parasitic wasps that help with aphid control.

Unlike warmer coastal and inland climates, where a late-summer heat spell ends bloom, our cool marine summer does not build enough sustained heat to shut this crop down early, so flowering runs from late spring to the first fall frost. Feed lightly on nitrogen, cut constantly, and remove pods to keep bloom coming. Watch for aphids, thrips, and powdery mildew in damp weather.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Chill is amply met in every zone here (this variety range needs 350 to 700 hours; the region banks far more), so the limiting factor is not cold, it is the cool, wet maritime spring. Apricot blooms earliest of any tree fruit grown here, and WSU's western Washington fruit handbook flags it as very sensitive to frost at bloom time; even where frost does not strike, cool, damp bloom-time weather keeps pollinators from working the flowers well and favors brown rot and coryneum blight on stone fruit generally. Reliable fruiting is genuinely site-dependent: the warmest, driest, most sheltered spot available, a late-blooming variety, and attentive dormant-season disease control are what turn a marginal crop into a real one.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Pawpaw hits its roughly 400 hour chill requirement here many times over, and WSU's western Washington fruit calendar includes it as an October-ripening crop, so this is a real, if late and marginal, Pacific Northwest fruit. The limiting factor is summer heat accumulation, not chill or cold hardiness: Kentucky State University's pawpaw program, the national authority on the crop, recommends early-ripening selections (Mango, Sunflower, Shenandoah, Potomac) specifically for low-heat-unit, cool-summer regions like this one, since a later-ripening selection is unlikely to finish before the season's first frost here. Plant two genetically distinct trees for pollination and shade young trees for their first couple of years.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8 west of the Cascades is too cold for an in-ground lemon. Lemon fruit and leaves are damaged once temperatures fall into the high 20s°F, and this zone's coldest nights drop well below that, into the teens or lower, so an unprotected tree does not make it through a typical winter, let alone one of the region's periodic harder freezes. Grow it as a container tree brought under cover for the coldest nights instead.

8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: WSU's own western-Washington fruit guidance notes that even a typically mild maritime winter brings a periodic harder frost some years; that is well within reach of zone 8's colder nights, and lemon is hurt at a far milder temperature than the hardy tree fruit this region is known for.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9's milder coastal and protected pockets sit closer to lemon's cold edge, and a container-grown tree (Improved Meyer is the hardier choice) can survive there long-term if it is moved under cover, or into a garage or bright room, whenever a hard freeze threatens. Even so, an occasional deeper freeze can still damage or kill an unprotected tree, so there is no dependable in-ground crop, only a protected container planting.

8.type_note_seasoned: Northern highbush is the blueberry to plant here. West of the Cascades, winters bank about 968 to 1,950 hours (average around 1,468) of winter chill, WSU Skagit County Extension station data, comfortably clearing this crop's roughly 1,000 hour chill requirement. The other real requirement is soil: native soils west of the Cascades are rarely acidic enough on their own, so start right by testing and amending to pH 4.5 to 5.5, or grow in containers or raised beds with an acidic mix (WSU).

Net the bushes against birds from mid-June through the end of harvest, and prune in the dormant season, winter into early spring, just before growth resumes. Plant at least two cultivars near each other for the best fruit set.
